title: Goldman or Morgan Stanley: Which Stock Is Better Bet Post Q3 Results? - TradingView
content: Wall Street heavyweights The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. GS and Morgan Stanley MS continue to capitalize on improving investment banking (IB) activity, robust equities trading and growing demand for financial services. Both companies delivered impressive third-quarter 2026 results, reflecting their strong market positions and ability to navigate a dynamic operating environment. The continued recovery in mergers and acquisitions (M&As), healthy underwriting activity, and strong institutional client engagement have supported their financial performances. While Goldman has demonstrated stronger IB revenue growth and trading momentum, Morgan Stanley continues to benefit from its diversified business model and expanding wealth management franchise. Against this backdrop, which IB powerhouse offers better investment prospects following the latest quarterly results? Let us examine. Goldman remains a dominant player in M&A advisory, underwriting and trading. The company's IB business has benefited significantly from improving global dealmaking activity and capital markets issuance. During the first nine months of 2026, IB fees jumped 40% year over year to $9.46 billion, supported by increases of 34%, 73% and 29% in advisory, equity underwriting and debt underwriting revenues, respectively. Management continues to view the capital markets environment favorably, with opportunities arising from strategic dealmaking, technology investments and AI infrastructure financing. Although higher interest rates and macroeconomic uncertainties could affect deal activity, GS's leading market position and healthy pipeline position it well to capitalize on the ongoing investment banking recovery. Goldman continues to streamline its operations by exiting non-core consumer banking businesses and strengthening its core franchises. The company is accelerating expansion in asset and wealth management to diversify its revenue sources and generate more durable fee-based income. In sync with these efforts, in August 2026, Goldman announced an agreement to acquire NEOS Investments, a provider of derivative income exchange-traded funds (ETFs). In April 2026, Goldman completed the acquisition of Innovator Capital Management, expanding its active exchange-traded fund (ETF) capabilities. Earlier, it completed the acquisition of Industry Ventures to strengthen its presence in venture capital and alternative investments. These initiatives complement its efforts to expand private market offerings and deepen client relationships. The benefits of Goldman's strategic repositioning are increasingly evident in its financial performance. For the first nine months of 2026, GBM revenues jumped 34% to $41.72 billion, while AWM revenues rose 15% to $13.73 billion. Continued asset gathering and strategic acquisitions should support recurring fee income and reduce the dependence on market-sensitive businesses over time. Morgan Stanley continues to leverage its integrated business model, encompassing institutional securities, wealth management and investment management. The company has strategically diversified its revenue streams to reduce the dependence on volatile capital markets activities while benefiting from improving IB conditions. The company's IB performance remained strong during the first nine months of 2026, with consolidated IB revenues increasing 30% year over year to $7.30 billion. The company is well-positioned to benefit from a healthier deal environment, supported by a robust and diversified pipeline across regions and sectors. Momentum is expanding beyond the Americas into Asia and EMEA, while active M&A and IPO markets, together with the company’s strong competitive position, are expected to support further growth as the macroeconomic backdrop evolves. Morgan Stanley's strategic focus on expanding wealth and investment management operations remains a major strength. Acquisitions such as E*TRADE and Eaton Vance have enhanced its scale and diversified its business mix. Further, the acquisition of EquityZen, completed in January 2026, strengthened its private markets capabilities and offerings for corporate and wealth management clients. The benefits of this transformation were evident in the first nine months of 2026. Wealth Management revenues increased 13.4% year over year to $26.44 billion. Moreover, the business attracted $498.9 billion in net new assets and $173.3 billion in fee-based asset flows during the first nine months of 2026. Wealth Management client assets reached $8.43 trillion as of September-end, up 19.5% year over year, while combined client assets across Wealth and Investment Management stood at $10.5 trillion, highlighting the growing scale of Morgan Stanley's wealth management franchise. This expanding client asset base provides Morgan Stanley with significant opportunities to generate recurring fee revenues and deepen client engagement. GS & MS: Price Performance, Valuation & Other Comparisons Over the past year, Goldman shares have gained 10.9%, outperforming Morgan Stanley’s 8.1% rise. In comparison, the industry has returned 3.3%. From a valuation perspective, Goldman appears relatively attractive. Its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio stands at 11.94X, below Morgan Stanley's 13.56X. The valuation discount suggests that Goldman offers a relatively attractive entry point, particularly given its stronger recent earnings growth. In terms of shareholder returns, both companies continue to prioritize dividends and share repurchases. Following the Federal Reserve's 2026 stress test, GS increased its quarterly common stock dividend 11% to $5 per share. Similarly, in July, the company increased its quarterly dividend 15% to $1.15 per share. Morgan Stanley offers a dividend yield of 2.56% compared with Goldman's 2.28%. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for GS’ 2026 and 2027 earnings indicate 38.1% and 4.3% growth, respectively. Earnings estimates for both years have been revised upward over the past month. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MS’ 2026 and 2027 earnings indicate 25.7% and 3.9% growth, respectively. Earnings estimates for both years have been revised upward over the past month. Both Goldman and Morgan Stanley remain well-positioned to benefit from the recovery in investment banking activity and growing demand for asset and wealth management services. Goldman's strong IB franchise, solid equities trading performance and strategic initiatives to expand its asset and wealth management operations should continue to support earnings growth. Its attractive valuation relative to Morgan Stanley offers a potential margin of safety, although elevated expenses and capital markets volatility remain concerning. Morgan Stanley, by contrast, offers greater earnings diversification, supported by its expanding wealth management franchise, recurring fee income and strong client asset inflows. Its superior dividend yield and solid capital position make it an attractive option for investors seeking a combination of growth and shareholder returns. However, its relatively expensive valuation could limit near-term upside. Overall, Goldman appears to be the more compelling investment choice at current levels. Its stronger earnings momentum, greater exposure to recovering investment banking activity and relatively favorable valuation position it for potentially higher returns. title: The Middleweight Adventure Bike That Delivers The GS Experience Without The GS Price - Top Speed
content: The GS badge has become shorthand for a serious adventure motorcycle, but that reputation comes with a premium price tag. BMW's F 900 GS combines a potent parallel-twin engine with off-road hardware and sophisticated rider aids, making it a natural benchmark for the middleweight ADV class. The question is how much of that performance you really need when your typical weekend involves winding back roads, the occasional gravel track, and a few hours in the saddle. There's a Japanese alternative that follows much of the same formula, including a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims, while asking for considerably less of your wallet. The BMW F 900 GS makes a convincing case for its premium positioning with its 895cc parallel-twin being the heart of the package. It makes 105 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 68.6 pound-feet of torque, which is plenty for a bike this size. It isn’t heavy, either. BMW lists the road-ready, fully fueled weight at about 482 pounds, helped along by a lightweight plastic fuel tank. The F 900 GS, however, carries a $14,495 MSRP plus $695 in destination, and that’s before you touch the options list or the accessory catalog. BMW also calls for premium fuel, so every fill-up costs a little more. Moreover, plenty of riders spend most of their time on pavement and gravel, so a chunk of that capability never gets used. You still pay for it, though. That gap is exactly where a Japanese parallel twin with a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims wants to live, at a much friendlier price. That bike is the Suzuki V-Strom 800DE. It’s Suzuki’s off-road-focused middleweight adventure bike, built around the same 776cc parallel twin that powers the GSX-8S. Don’t mistake it for a budget stand-in, either. The 2026 model carries an MSRP of $11,799, plus $700 destination. The F 900 GS lists at $14,495 plus $695. The gap lands at $2,696, or about 18 percent of the BMW’s price. And the base model gets most of the hardware covered below: the 21-inch front wheel, long-travel suspension, and a full electronics package. Want to load it up? The V-Strom 800DE Adventure lists at $13,249. It adds 37-liter aluminum side cases, an accessory bar, a skid plate, and remote-adjustable rear suspension. Even then, it still costs about $1,200 less than a base F 900 GS. Under the tank sits a liquid-cooled, DOHC 776cc parallel twin. Bore and stroke are 84 x 70 mm, compression is 12.8:1, and a six-speed gearbox sends power to the rear wheel via chain. A 270-degree crank gives it a V-twin-like feel, while Suzuki’s Cross Balancer (two counterbalancers set diagonally) keeps vibration down and the engine compact. Suzuki says it deliberately favored smooth, low-rpm torque over chasing peak power. The Suzuki produces a claimed 83 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 57.5 pound-feet of torque at 6,800 rpm. That leaves it approximately 22 horsepower and 11 pound-feet behind the BMW. This naturally makes the F 900 GS the quicker motorcycle. Its additional performance should be noticeable during hard acceleration, highway passing maneuvers, and spirited riding with luggage or a passenger. However, peak output doesn't tell the whole story. Reviews of the 800DE have praised its tractable power delivery and the way its Gravel traction-control setting allows controlled rear-wheel slip. Owner discussions similarly highlight its versatility on highways and dirt roads. For riders who value usable performance over outright acceleration, the Suzuki's engine makes a compelling case. Want something more road-focused? Both the F 900 GS and V-Strom 800DE enduro ADVs have adventure tourer alternatives. BMW offers the F 900 GS Adventure, which brings a larger fuel tank, improved wind protection, and an available Dynamic ESA electronic suspension. But tipping the scales at 542 pounds and starting at $15,195, it’s also the more expensive option. You don’t pay the same premium as the road-going V-Strom 800 base model, which starts at $10,294. This one features shorter suspension travel and basic spring preload adjustability, with cast wheels, the front being a 19-incher rather than a 21-incher. It also has a lower seat height, a street-focused windscreen, and non-switchable ABS. The Touring builds on this with a factory-installed topcase and handguards. If you prioritize road comfort over outright off-roading, the base V-Strom is a much better value than the F 900 GS Adventure. It's not as capable as the GS but will get the job done just fine. This is where the V-Strom really earns its keep. It rolls on a 21-inch front and a 17-inch rear spoked wheel, the same sizes as the BMW. Suspension travel is about 8.7 inches at both ends, with an inverted fork up front. BMW quotes 9.05 inches front and 8.46 inches rear for the F 900 GS, so it’s close to a wash. Ground clearance is 8.7 inches, the tallest in the V-Strom family. Suzuki even swept the muffler upward so it stays clear of all that long-travel suspension. That said, according to one reviewer, all that travel could mean a noticeable dive under hard braking that may take some getting used to. Weight is where you’ll notice a gap. The V-Strom’s curb weight is 507 pounds, while BMW lists 482 for the F 900 GS, fully fueled. Twenty-five pounds sounds small until you're picking it up out of a rut. Seat height tilts slightly in Suzuki’s favor. The V-Strom sits at 33.7 inches, against 34.2 inches for the standard F 900 GS. Half an inch might not sound like much, but it counts for shorter riders flat-footing at a stoplight. Suzuki covers the essentials well. The Suzuki Intelligent Ride System bundles three drive modes, traction control with a dedicated gravel setting, a rear-ABS-off option, and a standard bidirectional quick-shifter that leaves the clutch alone for most shifts. A five-inch color TFT display handles instrument duty. If you mostly want help on a dirt road, the Suzuki’s package covers the stuff that actually counts. Running costs tip toward Suzuki, too. Its 5.3-gallon tank also holds roughly 40 percent more than the F 900 GS’s 3.8 gallons, which helps when the next gas station sits a long way from the trailhead. The V-Strom’s weak spot is the warranty. Suzuki offers 12 months of limited coverage, versus BMW’s 36 months or 36,000 miles. But Suzuki bikes tend to outlast their European rivals, so that's the peace of mind you get with the V-Strom. Does the V-Strom 800DE give GS riders everything? Not quite. You give up some power, a few pounds, and warranty length. However, you keep the wheels, the travel, the clearance, and the electronics that matter off-road, and you keep $2,700 in your pocket. For plenty of weekend riders, that’s a trade worth making. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: Upcoming BMW F 650 GS Spotted Testing: Yamaha Tenere 700 Rival Incoming - ZigWheels.com
content: BMW Motorrad is working on a new adventure motorcycle that could take on the Yamaha Tenere 700 and KTM 790 Adventure in the international market. The upcoming ADV has been spotted testing abroad, giving us a fair idea of what to expect. While BMW has not revealed any details yet, the test images suggest that this could be an entirely new offering in its adventure bike lineup. The test motorcycle gets an X-shaped headlight design, which is becoming a familiar BMW styling element. The fairing also features cutouts for the BMW badges, making its identity quite obvious. Interestingly, its overall silhouette looks quite similar to the larger BMW F 900 GS, although the front section appears to be new. The motorcycle gets a tall stance, a slim body and what looks like a proper adventure-ready design. We expect BMW to offer multiple accessories, including a taller windscreen and other touring-focused equipment. The biggest highlight could be the new parallel-twin engine. BMW is expected to use a new 650 cc-700 cc motor, which could produce around 75 PS and 69 Nm. The fact that the motorcycle was spotted testing alongside the Tenere 700 and KTM 790 Adventure also gives us an idea of its intended positioning. If these figures are accurate, the new ADV should offer enough performance for highway touring while remaining manageable on rough roads and trails. The test motorcycle features an inverted fork at the front and a monoshock at the rear. It also gets tubeless spoke wheels at both ends, which should make it more practical for adventure touring. Braking duties are handled by dual discs at the front and a single disc at the rear. We also expect BMW to offer adjustable suspension and a comprehensive electronics package, potentially including multiple riding modes and other rider aids. However, the final specifications are yet to be revealed. BMW could unveil the new adventure motorcycle at EICMA 2026, with a market launch likely to take place sometime in 2027. If launched in India, it could become an interesting alternative to the middleweight adventure bikes currently available in the segment. BMW seems to be working on a more accessible adventure motorcycle that combines the familiar F 900 GS design with a new, smaller engine platform. title: Chocolate Glutinous Rice Cakes, Pizza White Rice Cakes Dominate Convenience Stores - 조선일보
content: Sales surge as CU, 7-Eleven, GS25 introduce innovative rice cakes blending traditional, Western flavors The competition in convenience store desserts is expanding into rice cakes. From glutinous rice cakes filled with chocolate to white rice cakes topped with pizza ingredients, unique products are continuously appearing on convenience store shelves. As the so-called "rice cake pilgrimage," where people visit popular rice cake shops, becomes a trend, and videos of tasting unique rice cakes gain popularity on social media, convenience stores are also increasing their rice cake offerings. According to the convenience store industry on October 26, CU’s rice cake sales from January to September this year increased by 96.5% compared to the same period last year. Following a 42.2% increase in 2024 and a 17.6% increase last year, this year’s growth nearly doubled. 7-Eleven also saw a 62% increase in rice cake sales during the same period this year, surpassing last year’s growth rate of 19%. Unique combinations of traditional rice cakes with Western ingredients such as chocolate, cream, and cheese are gaining popularity.   CU’s "Fresh Chocolate Mochi" and "Fresh Chocolate Matcha Mochi," released on September 16, surpassed 400,000 units sold in just one month. These products, which add chocolate to thin and chewy rice cakes, are priced at 3,200 Korean won each. As these products gained popularity, CU’s rice cake sales from October 1 to 22 increased by 158.9% compared to the same period last year. CU also launched the "Mochi Pave Chocolate Matcha Flavor" priced at 4,500 Korean won on the 22nd. A product with pizza toppings on rice cakes has also emerged. GS25 introduces "Snowflake Pizza Rice Cake," which features pizza sauce, cheese, pepperoni, and corn on top of white rice cake. This frozen product uses white rice cake instead of pizza dough and can be heated in a microwave. Priced at 3,900 Korean won for two pieces, it will accept 5,000 limited pre-orders via the "Our Neighborhood GS" app from October 26 to 31, with nationwide sales starting November 5. Traditional rice cakes are also gaining popularity and appearing as convenience store products. 7-Eleven will launch "Pumpkin Injeolmi Rice Cake" and "Black Sesame Rice Cake" on October 29, inspired by popular rice cake specialty shop menus. The Pumpkin Injeolmi Rice Cake is made with domestic glutinous rice and pumpkin powder, coated with castella crumbs. The Black Sesame Rice Cake is an Injeolmi rice cake filled with red bean paste and coated with black sesame powder. These combinations are known as representative products of Chang-eok Tteok, a rice cake shop in Gwangju. Each is priced at 3,500 Korean won. A source from CU stated, "Recently, desserts that provide visual pleasure as well as unique textures have been trending on social media, so we are actively reflecting these trends from the product development stage."

title: “We are not ship jumpers”, SODELPA GS tells PAP - The Fiji Times
content: SODELPA general secretary Levi Vere has hit out at the People’s Alliance Party (PAP), declaring that SODELPA does not need lessons on political loyalty because its members are not “ship jumpers”. Mr Vere accused PAP of attempting to lecture SODELPA on political timing and parliamentary numbers while overlooking the sacrifices made by the party during the Bainimarama administration. “We do not need lessons on loyalty because we are not ship jumpers,” Mr Vere said. He said SODELPA had stood virtually alone in opposing the Bainimarama government long before PAP emerged as a political party. “Long before PAP ever emerged as a political party, SODELPA stood virtually alone in the trenches fighting the Bainimarama regime.” Mr Vere claimed that since 2014, SODELPA members, particularly women and youths, had faced political persecution and public humiliation for defending indigenous rights. “Since 2014, while today’s so-called political champions were silent, compromised, or nowhere to be seen, SODELPA’s members, our youth, and our mothers paid dearly,” he said. “Our people faced political persecution, were hauled before the courts, and were shamed publicly for standing up for indigenous rights.” He also credited SODELPA with leading opposition to the former government’s proposal to change Fiji’s national flag. “Our youths and women fought the Bainimarama regime when it wanted to change our national flag,” he said. “SODELPA led the fight that saved our national flag and identity!” Mr Vere maintained that the party’s political standing was built on years of struggle rather than political convenience. “SODELPA earned its mandate through blood, sweat, tears, and relentless sacrifice—not through political convenience.” His comments come amid political differences between SODELPA and PAP over constitutional reform and parliamentary support.

title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Pinheiro Braathen Wins, Radamus Fourth - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, Marco Odermatt / GEPA pictures Three of the final four racers took the lead. The last man down the mountain won. Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen delivered a commanding victory in Sunday’s Sölden men’s World Cup giant slalom, defeating Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard and Marco Odermatt in a thrilling opening to the 2026-27 season. The reigning Olympic and World Cup GS champion entered the second run with a 0.24-second advantage. What followed was an extraordinary battle on the Rettenbach glacier. American River Radamus held the leader’s chair deep into the final seven before three of the last four starters took turns moving into first place. Pinheiro Braathen eventually prevailed by 0.48 seconds, while just one hundredth separated the two Swiss podium finishers. The reverse-30 second run had already produced remarkable performances and several lead changes before the leading contenders prepared to challenge. Radamus, who had started the afternoon tied for 15th, remained the overall leader when only seven racers were left. His exceptional second run had forced the biggest names in giant slalom to chase his time. Henrik Kristoffersen, seventh after Run 1, couldn’t find the necessary speed and eventually finished 22nd. Germany’s Fabian Gratz also fell short of Radamus’ mark. Norway’s Atle Lie McGrath, fifth after the opening run, fell on the upper pitch and failed to finish. Odermatt, fourth after Run 1, delivered the seventh-fastest second run. The Swiss star finally ended Radamus’ extended stay in the leader’s chair. “I made a big step in the second run: I found the race gear and that’s the most important thing,” Odermatt told FIS. His third-place finish would ultimately become his 47th World Cup GS podium, establishing a Swiss record. It was an encouraging start after an offseason affected by injury. Austria’s Stefan Brennsteiner was next. Third after the opening run, Brennsteiner couldn’t match the pace. His second run ranked 22nd, dropping him to 11th overall and guaranteeing Odermatt a podium. The Swiss skier had finished the first run 0.31 seconds ahead of his teammate. He needed to protect that advantage to take the lead. Although Odermatt recorded a faster second run, Meillard delivered a strong finishing section and crossed just 0.01 seconds ahead. The result was especially satisfying for Meillard, who had never previously finished higher than fifth at Sölden. “Sölden and me haven’t been friends in the last few years so to start the season with a podium and some solid skiing feels good,” Meillard told FIS. The narrow margin over his teammate added another layer of satisfaction. “I had a few times when I was one-hundredth behind, so now it’s my turn to be in the front,” Meillard said. Odermatt recognized that the ultimate challenge remained the Brazilian who had dominated the opening run. “Lucas was too fast in the first run for the victory today,” he acknowledged afterward. Meillard had the lead. Odermatt was guaranteed third. Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic and World Cup GS champion, stood at the start knowing the entire race would be decided by his final run. Lucas Pinheiro Braathen stood at the start knowing he was the only racer who could deny Meillard victory. The 26-year-old Brazilian had already established himself as the world’s leading giant slalom racer, winning Olympic GS gold and the discipline’s World Cup crystal globe last season. Pinheiro Braathen had dominated the shortened first run, opening a 0.24-second advantage over Meillard and a 0.55-second lead over Odermatt. The same reduced course length was used for Run 2. Both runs had become intense sprints, with less accumulated fatigue but little opportunity to recover lost time. He increased his overall advantage through the opening and middle sections, reaching the final sector with 0.61 seconds in hand over Meillard. The Swiss skier had been particularly strong on the closing stretch, and Pinheiro Braathen surrendered some of his advantage approaching the finish. Pinheiro Braathen crossed 0.48 seconds clear, securing his fifth World Cup giant slalom victory and 12th podium in the discipline. His second-run time ranked 10th fastest. Combined with his exceptional opening performance, however, it was more than enough. Three of the final four racers had taken the lead. The final starter had won. Pinheiro Braathen acknowledged the expectations he carried into Sölden. “There was a lot of pressure on my shoulders today,” he said in his finish-area interview. “Pressure is privilege, and I was able to capitalize off of that.” The victory marked a remarkable contrast to the previous year’s Sölden opener, when Pinheiro Braathen failed to finish. This time, the Atomic and Oakley athlete arrived as the reigning Olympic champion and World Cup GS titleholder. “What a relief to be able to open the show in this way,” he said. Pinheiro Braathen explained that he had spent the offseason searching for new ways to improve following his Olympic gold and crystal globe. Those achievements brought confidence rather than hesitation. “I didn’t want to hesitate. I knew what I had in me,” he said. The Brazilian also thanked his family, team and supporters, recognizing their contribution to his latest victory. For the United States, River Radamus delivered one of the most impressive performances of the afternoon. The only Stifel U.S. Ski Team racer to qualify for the second run, Radamus finished the opening run tied for 15th, 1.15 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. “I was disappointed in my first run because I don’t think that I showed the skiing that I’ve been working towards,” Radamus said afterward. With some of the pressure lifted, the American attacked and produced a time of 51.99 seconds, the second fastest of the afternoon. Only Austria’s Raphael Haaser, who recorded 51.90, skied faster. “But the pressure was off a bit the second run, and I was able to connect some of the good turns that I’ve been working on,” Radamus said. “I’m happy with the progress we’re showing.” The American was particularly effective through the middle sector, where he posted the fastest time in the field. Against Haaser, who was leading when Radamus started, he built a 0.45-second advantage by the final intermediate split. Radamus lost 0.41 seconds of that cushion on the final stretch but crossed just 0.04 seconds ahead of the Austrian. One challenger after another failed to beat his combined time of 1:45.54. When the final seven racers prepared to start, Radamus was still leading. His performance had transformed the race, forcing the sport’s biggest stars to beat a time established by a racer who had finished the opening run in 15th. Eleven subsequent starters failed to displace him before Odermatt finally took the lead. Radamus ultimately finished fourth, climbing 11 positions and missing the podium by 0.33 seconds. Radamus offered valuable insight into why the second run produced so many impressive climbs. “The course was almost the exact same,” he said. “We were in the same grooves for a lot of it, so we knew what to expect.” The shortened course featured relatively open turns, allowing racers to maintain speed and attack. “It was very easy, very open. The snow was great,” Radamus explained. “You couldn’t afford to slow yourself down at all. You had to go at it.” That approach proved particularly effective for racers who had started the afternoon outside the leading group. Radamus also acknowledged that conditions changed between runs. The snow became more mixed, while visibility and wind remained considerations on the mountain. “The snow changed a bit between runs. It was like sort of a spring mix in the second run,” he said. Rather than dwell on the changing conditions, Radamus focused on making the most of them. “I tried to take advantage and make the most of it.” His result provided an outstanding start to the season. Radamus said he planned to remain in Europe for super-G training before returning to the United States to prepare for the upcoming World Cup races at Copper Mountain. Britain’s Freddy Carrick-Smith provided another of the afternoon’s memorable performances. The 19-year-old started the opening run wearing bib 46 and qualified for his first World Cup second run in a tie for 21st place. That achievement alone was significant for British alpine racing. His afternoon performance made the occasion even more memorable. Carrick-Smith produced the fifth-fastest second run, stopping the clock at 52.21 seconds. He climbed nine positions to finish 12th, earning his first World Cup points. “Yeah, it was amazing,” Carrick-Smith said afterward. “I guess I couldn’t have asked for much more out of my first run and second run.” The young Briton acknowledged that finishing his second run had been a priority. He held back slightly rather than risk losing the opportunity. Even so, his competitive time ranked among the day’s strongest performances. His breakthrough recalls fellow British racer Charlie Raposo’s World Cup giant slalom results at Kranjska Gora in March 2022. For a teenager competing against the world’s best, 12th place represents a significant career milestone. Carrick-Smith also spoke about representing a country with relatively few World Cup alpine competitors. “There’s not many GB skiers. It’s just good to be an influence, I guess.” Austria’s Raphael Haaser delivered the fastest second run of the competition, recording 51.90 seconds. Starting the afternoon in 20th, Haaser climbed 15 places to finish fifth, just 0.04 seconds behind Radamus. France’s Léo Anguenot also enjoyed a remarkable afternoon. The French racer temporarily occupied the leader’s chair before finishing ninth, improving 14 places from his first-run position. Norway’s Rasmus Bakkevig, the reigning Junior World GS champion, delivered another exceptional performance. Starting with bib 49, Bakkevig qualified 29th in the opening run. He then produced the fourth-fastest second run, taking an early lead and holding it through five subsequent challengers. He eventually finished 14th, climbing 15 positions. Six athletes moved up at least 10 places during the second run. Finland’s Eduard Hallberg earns the Ski Racing Media Bibbo Award, recognizing the greatest numerical improvement from original starting bib to final finishing position. Hallberg started with bib 55 and finished 16th, a difference of 39 positions. The Finn also recorded the fastest final sector of the second run, demonstrating impressive speed over the closing stretch. Bakkevig deserves recognition as well. The young Norwegian started bib 49 and finished 14th, a difference of 35 positions. Both performances illustrate the opportunities available to racers starting deep in the field. Switzerland left Sölden with two podium finishers, while Norway failed to place a racer in the top 10 despite qualifying six athletes for the second run. For a nation accustomed to success in men’s giant slalom, the absence of a Norwegian among the leaders was unusual. Kristoffersen dropped from seventh to 22nd, while Lie McGrath failed to finish. However, Norway’s younger athletes delivered encouraging performances. Eirik Hystad Solberg climbed from 13th to eighth, while Bakkevig’s remarkable second run demonstrated the potential of the next generation. Germany also showed improving depth in giant slalom. Three German racers qualified for the second run. Gratz finished sixth, Grammel climbed from 30th to 15th, and Alexander Schmid placed 21st. Norway led all nations with six second-run qualifiers. Austria and Switzerland each qualified four, while seven nations had just one racer advance. The 2026-27 World Cup giant slalom season opened with seven overall lead changes, remarkable climbs and an extraordinary battle among the final four racers. But when the competition reached its decisive moment, the reigning champion delivered. Pinheiro Braathen defeated two of Switzerland’s most accomplished racers and demonstrated that last season’s Olympic gold and crystal globe had not diminished his ambition. The Brazilian opened the season with victory, leaving his rivals with an immediate challenge: finding a way to beat the world’s leading giant slalom racer. Special thanks to Ski Racing Media journalist Darka Sefcik Starnova for her on-site reporting in Sölden and finish-area interviews, bringing the athletes’ voices and perspectives directly into this story. Darka Sefcik Starnova has loved ski racing since childhood, when she also competed in children’s categories. She founded United Ski Fans as a safe space for alpine ski racing enthusiasts, both online and at the races. Through this project, she shares engaging content from the world of fandom, fan clubs, and grandstand fun — simply for the joy of it. Darka is especially dedicated to the fan clubs of Petra Vlhová and Lucas Pinheiro Braathen. She believes alpine skiing is a sport of love, where fans treat each other with kindness and many athletes serve as role models for the younger generation. In her professional life, Darka works in education, where she values healthy and positive role models just as strongly. If there was any suggestion that Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (BRA/Atomic) would suffer a letdown this season after his extraordinary success earlier this year, those fears have been put to rest at the first time of asking. The Brazilian won the season-opening Giant Slalom race in Sölden on Sunday, marking his fourth straight elite GS victory, including his Olympic triumph and the late-season wins that propelled him to the 2026 Crystal Globe. Leading after the first run, Pinheiro Braathen skied aggressively but calmly in the second run to cruise to a deserved victory by nearly half a second over Loïc Meillard (SUI/Rossignol, +0.48s) and Marco Odermatt (SUI/Stöckli, +0.49s). "There was a lot of pressure on my shoulders today," Pinheiro Braathen said, referencing the beginning of his title defense and the highly-anticipated resumption of his rivalry with former GS king Odermatt. "But pressure is privilege and I was able to capitalize on that. What a relief to be able to open the show in this way." After returning to the tour two years ago with Brazil following a year in retirement after his early career with Norway, the 26-year-old has methodically ticked off a series of firsts for the nation he now represents: first World Cup win, first Winter Olympic medal (and gold at that), first Crystal Globe. Having reached those dizzying heights in such a short time, the philosophical Pinheiro Braathen put a lot of thought over the off-season into what would come next. "I've been searching for new curiosities, new paths to evolve from last year's Olympic gold and the Globe," he said. "We're headed towards new goals, new objectives." Yet he produced the same brilliant skiing that has repeatedly propeled him to the top of the podium in recent times. When he crossed the finish line in first place, he emphatically yelled "Vamos!" into the camera. "Even already from the second half of last season, I was able to bring that freedom that came with being able to accomplish those results, and bring that spirit into the very first race (on Sunday)," he said. "I didn't want to hesitate, I knew what I had in me, and I'm so, so proud to put it out there." On a bumpy, windy course from the reserve state gate that reduced each run to under a minute, there was no room for errors or hesitation even as the skiers were trying to find the snow under their feet in their first race of the season. While Pinheiro Braathen mastered the conditions the best, the Swiss pair of Meillard and Odermatt showed they are not far from the top of their game, even at this early stage of the season. Meillard, in particular, tends to start slowly and work his way into the season, and he had never finished higher than fifth on the Rettenbach glacier before Sunday. "Sölden and me haven't been friends in the last few years so to start the season with a podium and some solid skiing feels good," he said. As the second-last skier on the mountain, he trailed provisional leader Odermatt at the final intermediate split, but used a scintillating closeout to overtake his teammate by the barest of margins in ski racing: one-hundredth of a second. "I had a few times when I was one-hundredth behind, so now it's my turn to be in the front," Meillard said. "I guess next race, it's him again, and that's the beauty of the sport." Odermatt, the four-time Giant Slalom title winner who lost his Olympic gold and his Crystal Globe to Pinheiro Braathen last season, was satisfied with third after having his pre-season affected by injury. "To start the season with a podium is always nice," he said. "I made a big step in the second run: I found the race gear and that's the most important thing." Odermatt's 47th World Cup Giant Slalom podium moved him ahead of Michael Von Gruenigen (SUI) and Vreni Schneider (SUI) for the most all-time among Swiss racers, and that podium was about the most he could have hoped for on this day. "Lucas was too fast in the first run for the victory today," Odermatt admitted. For Pinheiro Braathen, it was his second victory in Sölden after he triumphed in 2020 while racing for Norway, and the personal journey he has undertaken between those wins was not lost on him. "It's amazing to look back at being able to be the youngest winner here and to come and do it again," he said. "That's something very special for me. That very day here, when I was 20 years old, that changed my life." Six years later, racing under a different flag and with new perspectives on skiing and life, it all came together for the Brazilian on Sunday. "I was just able to be me, I was able to be so connected with myself, and it felt so fun to ski that second run," he said. "I knew that this was how I was supposed to feel. And that's the feeling that I chase every single day.

title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Pinheiro Braathen Leads Run 1 - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen returned to Sölden on Sunday, Oct. 25, and delivered the fastest first run of the men’s 2026-27 Alpine World Cup opener. Behind him, seven racers starting bib 31 or higher fought their way into the second run, transforming the battle for qualification. A year after failing to finish the opening giant slalom on the Rettenbach glacier, the Brazilian Olympic champion and reigning World Cup GS titleholder showed exactly why he enters the new season as the skier to beat. Racing on Atomic skis and wearing Oakley eyewear, Pinheiro Braathen clocked 52.40 seconds. Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard finished just 0.24 seconds behind, while Austria’s Stefan Brennsteiner took third at +0.49. Defending Sölden champion Marco Odermatt sits fourth, 0.55 behind the leader, setting up an intriguing second-run battle. Strong winds forced organizers to start at the top of the steep pitch, shortening the first run to about 53 seconds. Overcast skies reduced visibility, and organizers removed the usual banner above the finish due to wind concerns. U.S.-born Norwegian Atle Lie McGrath, racing on HEAD skis, became the first man to start a World Cup race in the new season. Austrian Stefan Brennsteiner quickly set a faster benchmark before his teammate, Marco Schwarz, disappointed the home crowd with an early mistake that ended his run. Schwartz said, “Conditions are great, no issue, good work. I just wanted to be in a very straight line and it didn’t work.” Starting fourth, the Brazilian delivered the fastest middle sector and established a lead that survived all 69 starters. Meillard offered the closest challenge. After struggling to find his best form early last season, the Swiss star produced an encouraging performance. He matched the fastest opening-sector time but surrendered most of his 0.24-second deficit near the finish. Odermatt, racing on Stöckli skis and Salomon boots, remained within striking distance but lost 0.29 seconds in the middle sector alone. Henrik Kristoffersen provided another revealing contrast. The Norwegian matched the fastest opening split but lost 0.58 seconds in the final sector, leaving him seventh. The opening group established the early contenders, but improving visibility soon created opportunities for the racers starting behind them. As the light improved, several later starters demonstrated that the early leaders were not beyond reach. Germany’s Fabian Gratz, wearing bib 10, moved into sixth. Then Italy’s Giovanni Borsotti delivered one of the morning’s strongest performances, charging into eighth from bib 29, just 0.79 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. Germany’s Alexander Schmid followed from bib 27, finishing ninth at +0.84. France’s Thibaut Favrot, starting 21st, claimed 10th after producing a final sector just 0.01 seconds slower than the leader. Croatia’s Filip Zubčić also offered an encouraging sign. After a difficult season and a switch to Nordica skis and Marker bindings, the proven GS contender finished 12th, only 0.98 seconds behind. Belgium’s Sam Maes, who trains with the Stifel U.S. Ski Team and races on Völkl skis, finished 11th at +0.92. River Radamus was the lone American to qualify, finishing tied for 15th, 1.15 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. The Stifel U.S. Ski Team racer initially crossed in 10th but gradually slipped as later starters delivered faster performances. Radamus has demonstrated the ability to produce exceptionally fast individual runs, leaving him an opportunity to attack in the afternoon. Great Britain’s 19-year-old Freddy Carrick-Smith delivered an even more dramatic performance. Starting bib 46, the young British racer charged into a tie for 21st, just 1.37 seconds behind the leader. He finished 25 positions ahead of his starting number, securing a rare World Cup giant slalom second run for Britain. The achievement recalls Charlie Raposo’s performance at Kranjska Gora in March 2022, when the British racer advanced to the second run and finished 27th. No Canadian, Japanese or South Korean racers qualified. The final starting group delivered one of the morning’s biggest surprises. With only one of the opening 30 racers failing to finish, opportunities appeared limited for those starting farther back. Yet seven racers wearing bib 31 or higher qualified for the second run, displacing several established competitors. Improving visibility helped create opportunities, but these athletes still needed exceptional execution to capitalize. Fastest high-bib qualifier: Sandvik, who finished 18th from bib 32. Highest bib to qualify: Hallberg, who started 55th and finished 26th. Biggest improvement: Hallberg also made the largest move, gaining 29 positions relative to his starting number. Italy’s Franzoni provided another remarkable highlight. Despite losing a full second in the middle sector, he produced the fastest final sector of the entire field, beating Pinheiro Braathen’s split by 0.13 seconds. The battle for qualification proved unforgiving. Ryder Sarchett of the Stifel U.S. Ski Team initially moved into 27th from bib 34, but later finishers pushed him outside the top 30. Seven successful high-bib qualifiers demonstrated the depth of the field and ensured that the opening race delivered drama well beyond the fight for the lead. The fastest 30 return in reverse order, with Pinheiro Braathen starting last. The Brazilian holds the advantage, but Meillard, Brennsteiner and Odermatt remain close enough to challenge. After a first run filled with surprises, the fight for the season’s opening World Cup victory is far from decided. title: Suns 131-122 Warriors (Oct 24, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: PHOENIX -- — Devin Booker scored 43 points, Miles Bridges added 16 and the Phoenix Suns won their home opener for the fifth straight season by beating the short-handed Golden State Warriors 131-122 on Saturday night. The Warriors — who were playing for the third time in four days — fell to 0-3 for the first time in 19 years while resting several key players, including Stephen Curry (right knee), Brandin Podziemski (low back), Draymond Green (low back) and Al Horford (low back). Booker scored 17 points in the third quarter and Jordan Goodwin hit a 3-pointer just before the buzzer to give the Suns a 102-92 lead entering the fourth. The Warriors hung around for a few more minutes, but the Suns eventually pulled away and Luke Kennard hit a 3 to extend the lead to 117-102 with six minutes left. Kennard finished with 11 points, hitting 3 of 5 from 3-point range, which is exactly what the team expected when they signed him in the offseason. Dillon Brooks had 15 points and five assists. The Suns were coming off an embarrassing 124-83 road loss in the season opener to the Trail Blazers. They struggled in the opening quarter of Saturday's game, too, making just 1 of 12 shots from 3-point range. But the shots finally started to fall and it was Booker who led the way. The five-time All-Star made 17 of 25 from the field and added seven assists and seven rebounds. Golden State was led by rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, who scored a season-high 26 points and made six 3-pointers. De'Anthony Melton added 25 points on 8 of 13 shooting. Booker scored 19 points in the first half, leading the Suns to a 57-54 halftime lead. Lendeborg had 13 for the Warriors. Suns: At Oklahoma City on Monday night.

title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Start List, Rankings, Times & How to Watch - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, Atle Lie McGrath / Sölden 2026 / GEPA pictures Lucas Pinheiro Braathen left Sölden last October without finishing the first run. By the end of the season, he owned the two biggest prizes available in giant slalom. The Brazilian won Olympic GS gold, captured the 2025-26 World Cup giant slalom title and closed the season with consecutive victories in Lillehammer and Kranjska Gora. Now Braathen returns to the Rettenbach glacier as the No. 1 skier on the GS World Cup Start List. The Atomic and Oakley athlete starts bib 4 Sunday and enters the 2026-27 opener as the man everyone else must beat. Defending Sölden champion Marco Odermatt starts bib 6, while Atle Lie McGrath opens the race with bib 1. The first men’s World Cup race of the season features 69 competitors from 24 nations. Pinheiro Braathen’s history with Sölden has taken several turns. He earned his first World Cup victory here in 2020 while representing Norway. Four years later, Sölden was where he scored Brazil’s first Alpine World Cup points. Last season brought another dramatic chapter. Pinheiro Braathen failed to finish the first run in Sölden, then produced the most successful GS season of his career. He won Brazil’s first Alpine World Cup Crystal Globe and brought the country its first Winter Olympic medal — and first gold — with his victory in the Milano Cortina giant slalom. He then won the final two World Cup giant slaloms in Lillehammer and Kranjska Gora. Pinheiro Braathen arrives on Sunday with five consecutive World Cup GS podiums and eight consecutive top-10 GS finishes. His World Cup career began with Norway, but his move to Brazil provided the path for him to continue racing after his break with the Norwegian system. He is now fully representing Brazil and has become one of the country’s most prominent winter-sport athletes. The Stöckli / Salomon skier won last year’s opener and has now won Sölden three times — in 2021, 2022 and 2025. A fourth victory on Sunday would tie American Ted Ligety for the most men’s World Cup GS wins in Sölden. Odermatt also makes his 200th World Cup start Sunday. He enters the season with 54 career World Cup victories and 102 podiums. His 29 career GS victories place him third on the men’s all-time list in the discipline. Braathen ended Odermatt’s run of four consecutive GS globes last winter. Their renewed battle begins immediately. The World Cup Start List and the current-season World Cup standings are different. The WCSL uses rolling results from previous races and helps determine start-order position. Because Sölden is the first giant slalom of 2026-27, there are no current-season GS standings yet. The top seven on the WCSL start Sunday in this bib order: Only four nations — Norway, Austria, Brazil and Switzerland — occupy the first seven WCSL positions. Switzerland and Norway have combined for 11 of the last 15 Sölden men’s GS podium positions. Odermatt won a tight race last October. The first four finished within four-tenths of a second. Radamus finished fourth in Sölden in 2024 and remains the highest-ranked American on the current GS WCSL. Sarchett earned his first World Cup GS top-10 last season when he finished 10th in Val d’Isère. Kenney enters the season with a different status and different equipment. He is an independent athlete competing as a Stifel U.S. Ski Team programmed athlete. He is coached by and trains with the U.S. team, but he is not a named team member and pays his own expenses. Kenney switched from Völkl/Marker to HEAD for this season and remains a SHRED athlete. Tommy Ford remains injured and will not race in Sölden. Sunday will be Paul Epstein’s first World Cup race as head coach of the Stifel U.S. Ski Team men’s technical program. Epstein previously ran the independent Global Racing program. That history creates an interesting connection inside Sunday’s race. Patrick Kenney raced with Global during his career. So did Belgium’s Sam Maes. Maes is now training with the Stifel U.S. Ski Team, giving American fans another athlete to follow this winter. Maes finished a career-best 12th in the World Cup GS standings last season. He recorded three top-seven finishes after never previously finishing inside the World Cup top seven. Read enters the season pursuing an 11th consecutive year scoring World Cup GS points. Sunday will also be his 204th World Cup start, moving him into fourth among Canadian Alpine racers, men and women combined, for career World Cup starts. Read has made seven previous Sölden starts. He has qualified for the second run four times and posted a career-best Sölden result of seventh in 2019. Carrick-Smith made his World Cup debut in last season’s Sölden giant slalom and returns for another opportunity on the Rettenbach glacier. Ski Racing Media has a significant and growing audience in Asia, particularly Japan and China. That makes Sunday’s late starters from Korea and Japan especially worth following. Both will attack from deep in the field, where adapting to changing course and snow conditions becomes increasingly important. Alexander Steen Olsen had been expected to make his World Cup return in Sölden after missing the entire 2025-26 season. Steen Olsen told Viaplay Norway that he had strongly hoped to race but concluded that he had not had enough preparation. “I’m a bit rusty on my skiing — I simply need more time,” he said. The Norwegian said he felt relieved after finally making the decision. He had been determined to start as long as his knee allowed it, but after missing an entire season, he decided more preparation was the better choice. Steen Olsen won the Sölden GS in 2024 and finished fourth in the season-long GS standings that winter. His immediate goal is now another training block before potentially returning in Levi. title: FC Seoul Ends Decade-Long Title Drought - 조선일보
content: GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo attends match as Seoul secures seventh K League 1 title [OSEN=Seoul World Cup Stadium, Reporter Jeong Seung-woo] A decade of waiting has ended. As FC Seoul finally returned to the summit of K League 1, GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo also visited Seoul World Cup Stadium in person to share the historic moment. FC Seoul drew 1-1 with Gangwon FC in the Hana Bank K League 1 2026 33rd Round match held at Seoul World Cup Stadium at 2 p.m. on the 24th. Seoul recorded 67 points (20 wins, 7 draws, 6 losses). At the same time, second-place Ulsan HD drew 2-2 with Pohang Steelers and remained at 51 points, allowing Seoul to clinch the title regardless of the results of the remaining five final-round matches. This is Seoul’s first title in 10 years since 2016. The club secured its seventh league championship in history, following previous titles in 1985, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2012, and 2016. A special guest attended the match at Seoul World Cup Stadium that day: GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo. Chairman Huh visited the stadium to watch the crucial match that could decide Seoul’s championship. The event gained additional significance as it coincided with an invitation extended to employees and families of GS Group affiliates, including GS Corp, GS Energy, and GS Engineering & Construction. Seoul’s final steps toward the title were far from smooth. In added time of the first half, Seoul faced a crisis when Kim Jin-su’s foul led to a penalty kick. However, goalkeeper Koo Sung-yun saved Kim Dae-won’s shot, preventing a goal. In the second half, Moon Sun-min, substituted in by Manager Kim Gi-dong, scored the opening goal in the 14th minute. He shook Gangwon’s net with a powerful right-foot shot after receiving a pass from Anderson. Although Gangwon’s Kang Joon-hyuk equalized five minutes later, making the score 1-1, Ulsan also failed to secure a win against Pohang. Seoul confirmed its 10-year title drought ended in front of its home fans. After the match, Chairman Huh Tae-soo personally encouraged the team. “Last time I visited, I asked for a healthy season without injuries, and you responded with a 10-year title,” Chairman Huh said, praising the players’ achievements. “I applaud your efforts. I want to share this joy with the fans who have longed for a championship,” he added. This title holds significant meaning not only for the club but also for GS Group. Chairman Huh has consistently emphasized “Fan First” and focused on improving fan services for FC Seoul. Notable initiatives include the FC Seoul mobile application, customer-oriented product development, and stadium facility improvements. Seoul also achieved success in attendance, surpassing an average of 22,000 people this season. It was a season that confirmed both the on-field result of a 10-year title and the continued support of fans. The reason Seoul’s title is particularly special is that the past decade was far from smooth. After winning the title in 2016, Seoul entered a long slump. In 2018, the team dropped to 11th place in the league and had to compete in the relegation playoff. The gap from the title race widened, contrasting with its reputation as a prestigious club in K League. The turning point came with Manager Kim Gi-dong’s appointment. Taking charge in 2024, Manager Kim led the team to fourth place in his first season. Although they finished sixth in 2025, this season marked the culmination of his third year with the championship. In a post-title press conference, Manager Kim said, “I remember saying when I came to Seoul, ‘I will restore the past glory of Seoul. I will win the title within three years.’ I’m happy we overcame difficulties and won. I’m also glad we kept our promise to the fans.” He emphasized, “This title was within my plan. I’m very happy, but it’s not the end. We must move toward another goal.” Seoul’s seventh title coincided with achievements by other GS Group-operated professional sports teams. Through its subsidiary GS Sports, the group operates FC Seoul and women’s professional volleyball team GS Caltex Kixx. GS Caltex won the 2026 Yeosu NH Nonghyup Cup last week. With FC Seoul lifting the K League 1 trophy, two GS Group-affiliated teams achieved back-to-back championships. The day held multiple meanings for Seoul: a title reclaimed after a decade, cheers from fans filling the stadium, and the group’s chairman’s on-site visit. The congratulatory message from Chairman Huh Tae-soo to the team was not just about the players’ on-field performance. It was a result shared with fans and club members who supported Seoul even during its long slump. Seoul now looks beyond this 10-year title and sets new goals. Manager Kim’s emphasis on continuous title competition and restoring the club’s status as a leader in K League remain key tasks. /reccos23@osen.co.kr

title: FC Seoul Clinches 10-Year Title with GS Chairman's Motivation - 조선일보
content: Chairman Huh Tae-soo's Fan-First Initiatives Help Club Achieve Record Attendance and Championship [Sangam = Sports Chosun Reporter Kim Ga-eul] Huh Tae-soo, chairman of GS Group, has become the 'championship fairy.' FC Seoul, led by manager Kim Ki-dong, drew 1-1 with Gangwon FC in the final regular league match of the 'Hana Bank K League 1 2026' held at Seoul World Cup Stadium on the 24th. Seoul recorded 21 wins, 6 draws, and 6 losses. At the same time, second-place Ulsan HD also drew 2-2 with Pohang Steelers, bringing the championship race to a close. Seoul erased the three-point gap to the champion and clinched the title for the first time in 10 years since 2016. Including the Anyang LG era, this is the club's seventh 'star.' A special guest was present at the stadium: Huh Tae-soo, chairman of GS Group. It was a clear motivation for the team. Captain Kim Jin-su said, "I sincerely appreciate the chairman’s visit. It’s true that his presence motivated us even more. With the championship right in front of us, I think that motivation was greater for us than for any other players today," adding, "As someone representing the team, we obviously achieved the desired result, so I expect a generous bonus. I believe the chairman will surely recognize our hard work." After the match, Chairman Huh said, "During my last visit, I asked for a healthy season without injuries. You responded with a championship after 10 years. I applaud your efforts and want to share today’s joy with the fans who have longed for this victory." He has consistently emphasized 'Fan first,' focusing on improving fan services such as the club’s mobile app, customer-oriented merchandise, and stadium facilities. Seoul surpassed an average attendance of 22,000 people in the league this season, achieving success in both performance and fandom. Sangam = Reporter Kim Ga-eul epi17@sportschosun.com

title: Moltzan wins after Shiffrin fades, first GS podium for Aicher - Yahoo Sports
content: American Paula Moltzan claimed a first World Cup career win and Germany's Emma Aicher reached a first giant slalom podium in third on Saturday as superstar Mikaela Shiffrin and others faded in deteriorating conditions. Moltzan shot from fifth after the first run to the top of the podium at the season opener on the Sölden glacier, pipping Lara Colturi, who missed a first ever World Cup victory for Albania, by one-hundredths of a second. Aicher was .52 back in third. Shiffrin topped the first run in search of her first giant slalom victory since December 2023 and a record extending 111th overall, but she had to settle for seventh in increasing snowfall and bad visibility. Swedish ace Lara Hector dropped from second to fourth and Swiss Camille Rast from third to sixth. Shiffrin beat Aicher by 87 points for the overall title last season but has said that she will ski fewer races in her pet event, the slalom, this year and mainly focus on giant slalom and super-g. That could help Aicher who like in the past plans to contest all races across the four disciplines. She has five World Cup wins in downhill and super-g and slalom podiums, and now finally also a podium in giant slalom. The 2023 team event world champion Moltzan meanwhile celebrated her first ever win after 10 podiums in the past. "It feels like a fairy tale, pretty unreal. I can't imagine a better start," she said. "We have put in a lot of hard work in summer." Last year's Sölden and discipline title winner Julia Scheib crashed out in the first run in front of her Austrian home crowd. The men's season opening giant slalom is on Sunday on the same hill.

title: Upcoming BMW F 650 GS Spotted Testing Abroad - BikeWale
content: BMW has been working on a new adventure bike that could be its answer to the Yamaha Ténéré 700. The motorcycle was spotted testing recently, and based on the images, we have a decent idea of what to expect: The X-shaped headlight section gives it away as a BMW, alongside the holes in the fairing where the BMW badging would be placed. Well, then there’s the BMW Motorrad jacket and riding pants that the riders are wearing. Apart from the new headlight section, the bikes overall silhouette looks quite similar to the BMW F 900 GS. The motorcycle will be powered by a new parallel-twin platform, likely going to be a 650cc-700cc mill. We think so because the motorcycle was spotted being tested along with the Yamaha Ténéré 700 and the KTM 790 Adventure. The motor is expected to make around 75bhp and 69Nm. Underpinnings-wise, the bike features an inverted fork and a monoshock. It rolls on tubeless spoke wheels at both ends, with braking duties taken care of by a dual-disc setup at the front and a single disc at the rear. Like the other models in the German bike maker’s lineup, we can expect this upcoming ADV to be offered with multiple accessories. A taller windscreen, adjustable suspension, and a more comprehensive electronic riding aids suite. The bike could be launched sometime in 2027, and the brand could unveil the bike at EICMA 2026.

title: Ridden: BMW F450 GS has come a long way, baby - Driven Car Guide
content: Please sign in to your account to add a vehicle to favourite Knobblier tyres and optional cross-spoke wheels finish off the F450 GS nicely. BMW Motorrad has long been aware that not everyone wants to buy a heavyweight adventure touring bike like the highly successful R1300 GS. It first surprised us with a “baby GS” 10 years ago when it released the underwhelming single-cylinder G310 GS in collaboration with its Indian partner, TVS, a decade ago. Now TVS and BMW have gone back to drawing board and built us a new twin-cylinder F450 GS with what feels like twice the horsepower. They’re taking the burgeoning lightweight ADV segment a lot more seriously this time. If only this brilliant 178kg bundle of riding fun had been the baby GS model that they released a decade ago. Perhaps because of the damage the G310 did to the GS brand, BMW hasn’t held back on the new technology it's incorporated into the new 450. There’s a new 420cc parallel twin with a unique 135-degree crankshaft, bringing a new inline twin-cylinder engine sound into a segment where Chinese twins favour 270-degree cranks because YouTubers keep telling the market they’re the best, and Japanese twins use 180-degree cranks because they rev more freely. Perhaps BMW should call this a 225-degree parallel twin. The piston of one cylinder reaches top dead centre (TDC) when the crankshaft has rotated 135 degrees, while the other does the same when the crank reaches 225 degrees of rotation. Calling it a 225-degree crankshaft positions the new layout nicely between the 180-degree and 270-degree twins of the BMW’s most direct rivals. Which is exactly how this lively new engine feels and sounds. It emits a gruffer exhaust signature than a 180-degree twin and is keener to rev out than a 270-degree motor. It represents the best of both crankshaft designs, I say. Next up, the ERC automatic clutch, fitted to the $14,490 Trophy model that is the flagship of the range. It’s standard equipment on the most expensive F450 GS, along with proper under-engine protection, handlebar risers, an extra riding mode for extreme off-road use, and rebound and compression damping adjusters added to the beefy 43mm front fork. It’s odd that the ERC is only standard on the priciest F450 GS, as it’s a feature most useful to rookie riders rather than those more experienced. Want the rest of the stuff fitted to the Trophy but not the ERC, the fancy paint, nor the alloy bashplate? Buy the $13,890 Sport version of F450 GS you see here. The $600 saving can then be put towards a set of cross-spoked wheels like the red test bike’s, an off-road durability enhancement that could cost as much as $2000 when the price is settled. Sitting at the bottom of the F450 GS range is the $13,490 Exclusive, which is still a well-equipped bike by lightweight ADV standards despite the entire range lacking cruise control. For it comes with BMW’s easy-to-read 6.5-inch TFT screen and all the brilliant switchgear design worthy of the badge. There’s IMU-enhanced traction control and ABS Pro, a decent selection of riding modes (minus Enduro Pro), adjustable hand levers, and a Type C USB socket. Excellent ergonomic tailoring is a feature of all three models. The seat height might look a bit daunting on paper at 845mm, but in practice it’s an easy bike to swing a leg over. The narrow width of the bike and the tapering of the rider’s seat towards the fuel tank make it easy to find a foothold when coming to a halt. Where the F450 GS really shines and justifies pricing that is a cut above many rivals, is its light, easy-to-ride dynamics. As a Learner-Approved Motorcycle the engine can’t make more than 48bhp, but the 178kg fully-fueled weight makes those brake horses feel like a team of thoroughbreds. There’s none of the top-heaviness that blights the handling of other welterweight ADVs. Not only is there about 20kg less mass than rivals like the Royal Enfield Himalayan 450 and the CF Moto 450MT, the BMW carries more of its mass lower. It feels beautifully balanced, both front to rear and top to bottom. Capping it off are the quality suspension and brakes. The former makes the most of the modest 180mm of wheel travel, the firm springs preventing it bottoming out on the big hits, and robust damping keeps the springs under control. Helped by radial caliper mounts and braided brake lines, the single front disc produces better stopping performance than the twin discs fitted to my Honda CB500X. Buy the Sport to get arguably the most value in the new F450 GS range, but don’t sweat the decision too much. Any of these three models makes a mighty fine “baby GS”.
